summaries.example: Imagine three things: a red ball, a red hat, and a red flower. They are different objects, but they seem to share something: redness. A platonist says redness is a real universal—a shared feature that exists independently of any one red object. A different philosopher might say only the individual red things exist, or that redness is just an idea we use.
summaries.summary: Platonism in metaphysics is the view that some abstract objects exist. In one common definition, abstract objects are not located in space or time, are not physical or mental, and do not cause events. Numbers are a familiar example: a platonist says that the number 3 is real and exists independently of people, even though it is not a physical object. Similar questions arise about properties such as redness, relations such as being north of, the meanings of sentences, sentence types, possible worlds, logical objects, and fictional characters. The entry compares platonism with several alternatives. Immanent realism says some of these things exist in the physical world. Conceptualism says they depend on minds, often as ideas. Nominalism says the things in question do not exist, even though we can speak meaningfully about them. Meinongianism distinguishes having some kind of being from existing, while non-factualism says there may be no fact of the matter about whether abstract objects exist. Arguments for platonism include the thought that shared properties explain similarities and the thought that true sentences about numbers seem to refer to numbers. The strongest challenge discussed is epistemological: if abstract objects cannot affect us, how can humans know about them?
key_ideas: Platonism says that some abstract objects really exist independently of human thoughts.
Numbers, properties, relations, propositions, sentence types, possible worlds, and fictional characters have all been discussed as possible abstract objects.
Other views say these things are physical, mental, nonexistent, useful fictions, or not matters with a definite fact of the matter.
The One Over Many argument says that shared features, such as redness, may explain why different objects resemble one another.
An ontological-commitment argument starts from ordinary true sentences, such as “3 is prime,” and asks what kinds of things those sentences seem to be about.
A major challenge asks how humans could know about abstract objects if humans live in the physical world and abstract objects do not.
summaries.why_it_matters: This debate helps us ask what kinds of things are real. It also shows that a simple sentence, such as “3 is prime” or “redness is shared by these objects,” can raise deep questions about language, mathematics, explanation, and knowledge. The different positions offer several ways to understand the same words without pretending that the disagreement has been settled.

important_terms.definition: A view that some real things, such as numbers or properties, are abstract objects that do not exist in space or time.
Something that is not in space or time, is not physical or mental, and does not cause physical events, according to one standard definition.
A feature that many different things can share, such as redness or being tall.
The view that there are no objects of the kind being discussed, such as numbers or properties.
The idea that numbers, properties, or other objects are mainly ideas in people’s minds.
A reason for doubting platonism: if abstract objects are outside space and time, how could people learn about them?

questions_to_think_about: When you say “3 is prime,” are you talking about a real thing, an idea, or something else?
Do three red objects need one shared thing called redness to explain their similarity?
Could a story be true about a character without that character existing like a person?
How could anyone learn about something that cannot be seen or touched?

summaries.example: Consider the true sentence “3 is prime.” A platonist reads “3” as referring to an object. Since the number 3 is not a physical or mental object, and since it is not located in space-time, the platonist concludes that it is abstract. A nominalist may instead say that the sentence is false if read literally, or that it can be replaced by a statement about a mathematical theory. A conceptualist may treat 3 as a mental construction, while an immanent realist may seek a physical-world account of mathematical objects.
summaries.summary: Platonism in metaphysics holds that abstract objects exist. On the entry’s standard working definition, such objects are outside space and time, non-physical, non-mental, and causally inert, although philosophers disagree about the correct definition. Numbers provide the clearest case: the platonist treats 3 as an objective entity rather than as a physical collection, a mental idea, or a convenient way of speaking. The same kind of realism can be extended to universals, including properties and relations; propositions understood as the contents of sentences; sentence types; possible worlds; logical objects; and fictional characters. One need not be a platonist about every category. The main alternatives form a taxonomy rather than a single anti-platonist doctrine. Immanent realism places relevant entities in the physical world. Conceptualism makes them mind-dependent. Nominalism denies that the alleged entities exist, though it includes several strategies for handling ordinary discourse. Meinongianism allows objects to have a kind of being without existing in the ordinary sense. Non-factualism denies that there is a determinate fact about whether abstract objects exist, or treats some existence claims as language-dependent. The One Over Many argument infers a shared property from the resemblance of particulars, but the entry explains why this may not add explanatory power. Ontological-commitment arguments are more influential: if true sentences such as “3 is prime” have a logical form that refers to an object, and if numbers are neither physical nor mental, platonism follows. key_ideas: The central issue is ontological: do numbers, universals, propositions, and related entities exist at all, and if so, what are they?
The taxonomy distinguishes views that accept the objects but locate them in the physical or mental world from views that reject them or reinterpret the relevant language.

The One Over Many argument treats a shared property as a possible explanation of why different particulars resemble one another, but nominalists can appeal to basic facts or deny that properties add explanatory value.
Ontological-commitment arguments reason from apparently true sentences to the entities those sentences seem to refer to. The argument for numbers uses claims such as “3 is prime.”

Anti-platonist responses may reject the truth of mathematical sentences, reject their face-value interpretation, reject the usual criterion of commitment, or regard existence claims as true by linguistic convention.
The epistemological argument presses platonists to explain how humans can acquire mathematical knowledge without causal or perceptual access to abstract objects.
summaries.why_it_matters: The issue connects metaphysics with mathematics, semantics, logic, linguistics, fiction, and epistemology. It forces a distinction between what language appears to refer to and what a theory must ultimately accept as real. It also illustrates a broader philosophical problem: a theory may seem to explain the objectivity and usefulness of a subject while creating a new puzzle about how we could know its entities.

important_terms.definition: The metaphysical position that abstract objects exist independently of human minds and physical space-time; the exact definition of “abstract” is debated.
An object characterized, on one standard account, as non-spatial, non-temporal, non-physical, non-mental, and causally inert.
A general property or relation that can be exemplified by many particulars, such as redness or being north of.
A principle about what entities a speaker must accept when accepting a literally true sentence, especially entities referred to by unavoidable singular terms or existential quantifiers.
The view that properties or mathematical objects exist in physical things or in the physical world rather than in a separate abstract realm.
The view that alleged abstract objects depend on minds, often as mental representations or ideas.
The view that the alleged objects under discussion do not exist; some versions reinterpret or fictionalize the relevant discourse.
The argument that knowledge of abstract objects seems difficult to explain because humans exist in space-time while abstract objects do not.

questions_to_think_about: Does the truth of “3 is prime” require a number 3, or can the sentence be paraphrased without referring to one?
Is saying that an object has a property genuinely explanatory, or does it merely restate that the object has that feature?
Should a true belief report refer to a proposition, or could it refer to a sentence-token or a mental representation?
Can mathematical theories be justified by their role in successful empirical science?
Does a theory become more credible when it explains more, even if it adds abstract entities?

summaries.example: Suppose your class has a red backpack, a red apple, and a red pencil case. One philosopher might say they resemble one another because they all have one shared property: redness. Another might say there are only three red objects, and no extra thing called redness is needed. A third might say redness is an idea people use to group objects. These answers resemble the main choices in the debate about abstract objects.
summaries.summary: The entry examines platonism, the view that abstract objects exist independently of our minds. An abstract object is usually described as something that is not in space or time, is not made of physical matter, is not a mind or an idea, and does not cause events. The number 3 is a standard example. According to platonism, 3 is real, but it is not a pebble, a group of three pebbles, or an idea in someone’s head. Properties and relations may also be treated as abstract. Red objects are physical, while redness would be a shared universal that many objects exemplify. The debate can be organized into several positions. Immanent realism agrees that the relevant things exist independently of us but places them in the physical world. Conceptualism treats them as mind-dependent. Nominalism says there is no extra object such as redness or the number 3. Meinongianism says that some objects have a kind of being without existing in the ordinary way. Non-factualism says there may be no definite fact about whether abstract objects exist. Two major arguments for platonism are discussed. The One Over Many argument begins with several similar things and proposes one shared property as their explanation. Critics reply that this may simply rename the feature or stop the search for an explanation rather than complete it. The ontological-commitment argument starts with apparently true claims such as “3 is prime” and argues that their ordinary grammatical form refers to a number. If numbers are neither physical nor mental, they must be abstract. key_ideas: Platonists believe that some abstract objects are real, even though they cannot be located like ordinary physical objects.
The debate includes numbers, properties, relations, meanings, sentence types, possible worlds, logical objects, and fictional characters.
Immanent realism and conceptualism accept some of these objects but place them in the physical or mental world; nominalism rejects them.
The One Over Many argument says a shared property might explain why different objects are alike.
An ontological-commitment argument asks what a true sentence appears to refer to, as in “3 is prime.”
The epistemological argument questions how humans can gain knowledge of abstract objects.
summaries.why_it_matters: This topic matters because it asks what our most familiar ideas—numbers, colors, meanings, and stories—are really about. It also shows why philosophers can agree that a sentence is useful or true-seeming while disagreeing about the objects behind it. Studying the debate helps separate questions about language, reality, explanation, and knowledge.

important_terms.definition: The view that some nonphysical things, such as numbers or properties, exist independently of human minds.
A thing that does not occupy a place or moment in the physical world; examples proposed in the debate include numbers and properties.
A feature or relationship that can belong to many different things, such as redness or being taller than.
The view that properties or numbers exist in physical things or physical arrangements.
The view that numbers, properties, or similar things are dependent on minds, often as mental ideas.
The view that there are no numbers, universals, or other alleged abstract objects of the relevant kind.
A rule for deciding what a sentence commits us to believing exists.
A challenge asking how people could know abstract objects if those objects are outside space and time.

questions_to_think_about: Are numbers discovered, invented, or something in between?
Does “red” name a shared property, or is it simply a useful word for many similar objects?
If two people speak different languages but believe the same thing, what is the object of their belief?
Can a fictional character be discussed truly without existing as a real person?
